title: Jan van Eyck signed the Arnolfini Portrait on the wall: ‘Jan van Eyck was here 1434’

cover.alt: Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait: a man in a dark fur-trimmed robe and wide hat holds the hand of a woman in a green gown in a bedroom, with a small dog at their feet, a brass chandelier above and a round convex mirror on the back wall.

body: Above the convex mirror in his 1434 double portrait, Jan van Eyck painted the Latin words *Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434*, ‘Jan van Eyck was here 1434’, in an ornate script more like a legal document than a painter’s signature. The mirror reflects the backs of the couple and two tiny figures in the doorway, one in red who is presumably the artist. The art historian Erwin Panofsky argued in 1934 that the picture records a marriage, with the painter as witness; others read it as a betrothal, a legal mandate or a memorial, and some think the inscription is simply a decorative flourish of the period. The oil painting on oak, 82.2 by 60 cm, has hung in London’s National Gallery since 1842.

slides.alt: Detail of the Arnolfini Portrait: the round convex mirror reflecting the couple from behind and two figures in a doorway, with the ornate inscription ‘Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434’ painted on the wall above it.
slides.caption: The mirror and the inscription. Tiny medallions around the mirror’s frame show scenes from the Passion of Christ.

slides.prompt: Who are the two tiny figures reflected in the doorway?
slides.answer: Two visitors; the one in red is presumably Van Eyck
slides.detail: They stand where a viewer would stand. The art historian Erwin Panofsky saw them as witnesses to a wedding, with the signature as the painter’s notarial stamp.

steps.label: A couple takes vows in a private room
Two witnesses appear in the mirror
Van Eyck signs the wall like a notary
The painting serves as the record

slides.heading: Objects loaded with meaning
items: One lit candle: marriage custom, or the eye of God
A little dog: fidelity, or just a lap pet
Oranges: wealth, and fertility in Italy
Her gathered gown: fashion, not pregnancy

slides.question: What did Panofsky think the painting was?
options: A portrait of the painter’s parents
An advert for a cloth merchant
slides.explanation: Panofsky (1934) read it as a marriage certificate in paint, with the signature as notarial authentication. Later scholars have proposed a betrothal, a legal mandate or a memorial portrait.

left.label: It looks like it
left.text: Her hand rests on a full, gathered green gown, and viewers have long assumed she is expecting.

right.label: Scholars say no
right.text: Gathered gowns were the fashion of the day, and virgin saints were painted in the same pose. Even the couple’s identity is debated.
